newsitem.title: USA: Surprise, but few trades, post-Commerce correction.
newsitem.headline: Surprise, but few trades, post-Commerce correction.

text.p: Currency market players were baffled, oblivious and dismissive of a sharp correction to the Commerce Department's U.S. trade report on Friday, ultimately finding few reasons to trade on a day-old figure even if it had changed substantially.

Commerce announced late Thursday that "reporting errors" on crude oil imports incorrectly exaggerated the size of the overall U.S. trade deficit for February, which was originally reported at a wider-than-expected $11.59 billion.

The corrected figure -- released after trading had wound down in New York and before Tokyo currency dealing had begun -- showed a gap of $10.4 billion, only slightly above original Wall Street forecasts for a $10.1 billion shortfall.

The smaller gap should have been dollar-supportive, but in Asia, traders appeared more preoccupied with remarks from key Japanese Ministry of Finance official Eisuke Sakakibara and pushed the greenback lower. The dollar recovered its losses against the yen by the time U.S. trading began, opening unchanged from Thursday's closing rate of 125.90/95 and clearly unfazed by the Commerce Department's amendment.
"It hasn't had any impact which is curious to me," said Stephen Jury, chief dealer at Union Bank of Switzerland. "If that had been the headline number yesterday, people would have bought the dollar."
Explanations for the market's lackluster response to the revised figures varied from the timing of the correction to the direction of the revision and the market reaction to the initial figures.

"The original reaction to the number was favorable, despite the high level and this only marginally changes the story, without changing the direction of the variables," said John Rothfield, international economist at NationsBanc-CRT.
He attributed Thursday's reaction to the strong 4.0 percent gain in exports -- a figure that was unchanged by the revisions.

Commerce Undersecretary Everett Ehrlich said on Friday the corrected number meant the addition of a "few tenths" of a percent to first quarter gross domestic product (GDP) estimates, predicting stronger growth than the robust 3.8 percent seen in the fourth quarter of 1996.
But these "few tenths" proved negligible for U.S. currency market participants, who were already heading home by the time Commerce's correction hit news wires.
"Given the timing of the revision, you couldn't really do much with it," said Hillel Waxman, chief foreign exchange dealer at Bank Leumi Trust Co of New York.
"The only place you could trade it was Japan and that's a stilted market which is limited in its scope," he added. "By the time you got to Europe it was yesterday's news."
